questions.prompt: What is the practical difference between a container and a virtual machine?

options.text: Containers share the host kernel; VMs run their own
Containers cannot run Linux workloads
VMs start faster than containers
Containers provide stronger isolation than VMs

questions.explanation: Sharing the kernel is why containers start in milliseconds and are far smaller. It is also why their isolation is weaker than a VM's hardware-level boundary.

questions.prompt: Why does ordering Dockerfile instructions carefully matter?

options.text: Docker requires COPY before RUN
Each instruction is a cached layer, invalidated by everything after a change
Instructions run in parallel otherwise
The order determines the container's user

questions.explanation: Copying source before installing dependencies means every code edit busts the dependency layer and reinstalls everything. Copying the manifest first keeps that layer cached.

questions.prompt: In Kubernetes, what is a Pod?

options.text: A physical machine in the cluster
A storage volume shared across nodes
The smallest deployable unit, holding one or more containers
A network policy applied to a namespace

questions.explanation: Containers in a Pod share a network namespace and can share volumes, so they are always scheduled together. Kubernetes schedules Pods, never bare containers.

questions.prompt: What does infrastructure as code give you over clicking through a console?

options.text: Cheaper cloud pricing
Automatic security patching
Faster network throughput
Reviewable, versioned, reproducible environments

questions.explanation: Declared infrastructure can be diffed, reviewed and recreated identically. Console changes leave no history, which is how environments drift until a deploy fails only in production.

questions.prompt: What is the point of a blue-green deployment?

options.text: It halves infrastructure cost during a release
It switches traffic between two environments so rollback is instant
It deploys to two cloud providers at once
It runs tests against production data

questions.explanation: The new version is deployed alongside the old and traffic is cut over once healthy. Rolling back is another traffic switch rather than a redeploy.

questions.prompt: Why should a container image not bake in secrets at build time?

options.text: Secrets increase the image size significantly
Docker strips environment variables on push
The secret remains in the image layers for anyone who can pull it
Build arguments cannot hold long strings

questions.explanation: Layers are immutable and inspectable, so a secret persists even if a later layer deletes it. Secrets belong in the runtime environment or a secrets manager.

questions.prompt: In AWS, what does a security group control?

options.text: IAM permissions for a user
Which regions a resource may be created in
Encryption keys for a bucket
Inbound and outbound traffic rules for a resource

questions.explanation: A security group is a stateful virtual firewall attached to an instance or interface. IAM governs who may call the API; a security group governs packets.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between high availability and durability?

options.text: Availability means the service responds; durability means the data survives
They are two measures of the same property
Durability applies only to compute resources
Availability is measured in bytes

questions.explanation: A store can be highly durable yet briefly unavailable during failover. Confusing them leads to designs that protect uptime but still lose data on a node failure.

questions.prompt: What does a Kubernetes readiness probe do?

options.text: Restarts the container if it fails
Decides whether the Pod should receive traffic
Checks that the image was pulled successfully
Verifies resource limits are within quota

questions.explanation: Readiness gates traffic; liveness restarts a hung container. Using liveness where readiness is meant turns a slow start into a crash loop.

questions.prompt: Why is a CI pipeline run on every pull request rather than only before release?

options.text: It reduces the number of branches
It is required for merging in Git
Failures surface while the change is small and fresh
It compiles faster on smaller changes

questions.explanation: Catching a break at the commit that caused it makes the cause obvious. Batching a month of changes means bisecting a large diff under release pressure.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a load balancer health check?

options.text: To measure response latency for billing
To stop routing traffic to an unhealthy instance
To scale the instance vertically
To rotate TLS certificates

questions.explanation: Instances that fail the check are removed from rotation, so users are not served errors. A check that only returns 200 without testing dependencies gives false confidence.

questions.prompt: What does autoscaling based on CPU fail to handle well?

options.text: Steady, predictable traffic
Gradual daily traffic growth
A workload bounded by I/O or a downstream limit
Instances of differing sizes

questions.explanation: If requests queue waiting on a database, CPU stays low while latency climbs, so no scaling happens. Queue depth or latency is the better signal, and more instances may worsen it.

questions.prompt: Why should logs be shipped off the instance that produced them?

options.text: Local disks cannot store text files
The instance may be replaced, taking the logs with it
Logging locally is not permitted in the cloud
Shipped logs are automatically anonymised

questions.explanation: Ephemeral instances are terminated on scale-in or failure, exactly when the logs matter most. Centralising them also makes correlation across instances possible.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of an overly broad IAM policy such as Action: '*'?

options.text: It slows down every API call
It prevents the resource from being deleted
A compromise of that identity grants full account access
It increases the monthly bill directly

questions.explanation: A wildcard removes any boundary, so one leaked key becomes an account takeover. Policies should name the actions and resources the workload actually uses.

questions.prompt: What does idempotency mean for a configuration management tool?

options.text: Applying the same configuration repeatedly leaves the same state
Each run must be executed only once
Configuration is applied in random order
Changes are rolled back after each run

questions.explanation: The tool converges toward a declared state rather than blindly running commands, so re-running is safe. That is what makes automated remediation possible.

questions.prompt: Why is a multi-stage Docker build useful?

options.text: It allows two containers to run in one image
It parallelises the build across cores
It automatically scans for vulnerabilities
Build tools stay out of the final image, keeping it small

questions.explanation: Compilers and dev dependencies live in an earlier stage, and only the built artefact is copied forward. Smaller images pull faster and expose less attack surface.

questions.prompt: What does the term immutable infrastructure describe?

options.text: Servers are replaced rather than modified in place
Infrastructure cannot be deleted once created
Configuration files are read-only
The cloud provider prevents manual changes

questions.explanation: A new image is built and rolled out instead of patching live servers, so every instance is identical and reproducible. It removes configuration drift as a category of failure.

questions.prompt: What problem does a service mesh address?

options.text: Compiling services written in different languages
Service-to-service traffic concerns like retries, mTLS and observability
Storing shared configuration files
Provisioning the underlying virtual machines

questions.explanation: A sidecar proxy handles routing, retries, encryption and telemetry uniformly, so each service does not reimplement them. The cost is real operational complexity.

questions.prompt: Why alert on symptoms such as error rate rather than on CPU usage?

options.text: CPU metrics are expensive to collect
CPU cannot be measured in containers
Symptoms reflect user impact; high CPU alone may be harmless
Error rates are easier to graph

questions.explanation: A busy CPU may be a healthy service working hard. Alerting on user-visible symptoms avoids waking someone for a condition that harms nobody, which is how alert fatigue starts.

questions.prompt: What is a rolling update in Kubernetes?

options.text: All Pods are replaced simultaneously
Pods are replaced gradually while the service stays up
The cluster nodes are rebooted in sequence
Traffic is mirrored to a second cluster

questions.explanation: New Pods come up and old ones drain within surge and unavailability limits, so capacity is maintained. It requires the two versions to be compatible during the overlap.

questions.prompt: What does a cloud provider's shared responsibility model mean?

options.text: The provider secures everything by default
Security is shared with other tenants
Responsibility is split between customers and support
The provider secures the infrastructure; you secure what you run on it

questions.explanation: The provider handles physical and hypervisor security. Access policies, patching your instances and not exposing a bucket publicly remain your responsibility.

questions.prompt: Why is a stateless application easier to scale horizontally?

options.text: It uses less CPU per request
Any instance can serve any request
It does not need a database
It can run without a load balancer

questions.explanation: With no local state, instances are interchangeable, so adding and removing them is safe. Session affinity is a workaround that reintroduces the coupling.

questions.prompt: What causes a surprise cloud bill most often in a student project?

options.text: Too many IAM users created
Using more than one region
Resources left running, plus egress traffic
Enabling multi-factor authentication

questions.explanation: Idle instances, unattached volumes and load balancers bill by the hour regardless of use, and data leaving the provider is charged per gigabyte. Budget alerts catch it early.

questions.prompt: What is the purpose of a canary release?

options.text: Sending a small share of traffic to the new version first
Deploying only during low-traffic hours
Running the new version with no traffic at all
Releasing to internal staff only, permanently

questions.explanation: A small slice of real traffic exposes problems that staging misses, while limiting the number of users affected. It requires metrics good enough to judge the canary.

questions.prompt: Why is a git-based workflow used to trigger deployments in GitOps?

options.text: Git is faster than a deployment API
It removes the need for a build step
The repository becomes the auditable source of truth for desired state
Git can store container images efficiently

questions.explanation: Desired state lives in version control, so every change is reviewed, attributable and revertible, and a controller reconciles the cluster toward it continuously.
